stories.headline: Two killed in Thornton double shooting; RTD train strikes police truck at scene
stories.summary:
Two people were shot and killed early Friday in Thornton after a vehicle crashed into a pole along Colorado Boulevard between East 100th Avenue and Thornton Parkway. Officers responded to a 911 call at 4:53 a.m. and found a male passenger dead at the scene and a female driver with life-threatening injuries; she died several hours later at a hospital.

The shooting complicated the police response when a Thornton officer left a department pickup truck on RTD N-Line train tracks, and an RTD train struck the empty vehicle at 6:34 a.m. No one was injured in the collision, but N-Line passengers had to disembark and were transferred to buses for roughly four hours before train service resumed at 10:45 a.m.

Colorado State Patrol is leading the investigation into the vehicle-train collision, while Thornton police launched a separate administrative review to determine whether the officer complied with department policy. Detectives are still working to determine exactly where the shooting took place before the vehicle crashed.

stories.headline: Pedestrian struck and killed by hit-and-run driver on I-270 exit ramp in Commerce City
stories.summary:
A 45-year-old man was struck and killed by a hit-and-run driver Thursday night while crossing back and forth through traffic on an off-ramp from Interstate 270 to Interstate 76 in Commerce City. The crash occurred around 8:30 p.m., and witnesses told Colorado State Patrol the man had been moving repeatedly across the roadway before he was hit.

The driver who initially struck the man fled the scene without stopping. A second driver later struck the man's body on the ramp but remained at the scene and cooperated with investigators.

Authorities had not publicly identified the victim as of Friday and have not said why he was on the exit ramp. Investigators were also unable to provide a description of the vehicle involved in the fatal hit-and-run.

stories.headline: Organized theft ring using 'booster skirts' to steal from Douglas County retailers
stories.summary:
Douglas County law enforcement is seeking the public's help to identify members of an organized retail theft ring that has been using so-called booster skirts to smuggle merchandise out of stores. The skirts are specially constructed garments lined with materials designed to defeat electronic security tags, allowing thieves to conceal large quantities of products.

The thefts occurred last month across the metro area, and investigators say the ring has been operating at a high volume. Law enforcement has released information about the suspects and is asking anyone with knowledge of their identities to come forward.

Organized retail crime has been a growing concern across the Denver metro area, with retailers and law enforcement agencies working to coordinate responses to increasingly sophisticated theft operations.

stories.headline: Colorado will not face water supply cuts under new federal Colorado River operating plan
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of the Interior on Friday released its highly anticipated operating plan for the Colorado River, confirming that Colorado and the other Upper Basin states — New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming — will face no mandatory water supply cuts for at least the next two years. The plan instead focuses cuts of 1.25 million acre-feet per year on the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California and Nevada.

Rather than a traditional long-term operating agreement, federal authorities created a 10-year framework requiring the operating rules to be renegotiated every two years. The seven Colorado River basin states failed to reach consensus on a longer-term plan, forcing the federal government to implement its own guidelines for the critical waterway.

Colorado draws significantly on the Colorado River for Western Slope agriculture, Front Range municipal water supplies, recreation and wildlife habitat. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum noted that 40 million people and millions of acres of farmland across the American West depend on the river's allocation. States may substitute a consensus long-term plan at any point during the 10-year framework if they can reach agreement.

stories.headline: Denver's 16th Street renovation lacked transparency and oversight, city auditor finds
stories.summary:
Denver City Auditor Timothy O'Brien released a report Thursday finding that the city's Department of Transportation and Infrastructure failed to maintain adequate transparency and oversight during the 16th Street renovation project. Among the key findings: city officials did not flag the known risk of unmapped historic brick sewers in project documents, even though the city was aware of 69 miles of such infrastructure dating to the 1880s. When construction crews uncovered part of that system, it added $18 million and nearly a year of delays.

City officials accepted a settlement and paid the additional $18 million to contractor PCL Construction, but routed the change as a 'change order' rather than a contract amendment — a distinction that allowed them to bypass City Council approval. The auditor recommended updating project systems so the Council can review costly changes; city staff disagreed with that recommendation.

Councilmembers Shontel Lewis and Chris Hinds, who sit on the transportation and infrastructure committee, told the auditor's office they were not kept adequately informed about deteriorating project conditions. The project's total cost rose from $149 million to $175 million as a result of various changes.

stories.headline: Downtown Denver revival leader Bill Mosher steps down; city charts next steps
stories.summary:
Bill Mosher, the veteran developer Mayor Mike Johnston recruited to lead downtown Denver's recovery and other major city projects, stepped down on Aug. 14 after about a year in the role. Mosher, who turns 76 in October, said the assignment had stretched beyond its original one-year scope and that he was confident in the plans and personnel left in place to carry the work forward.

Mosher's primary charge was revitalizing a struggling downtown while also helping oversee the conversion of Burnham Yard into the future home of the Denver Broncos. His central recommendation for upper downtown is converting it from a traditional central business district into a mixed-use residential neighborhood, arguing the city needs to add 10,000 residential units over the next decade.

He cautioned that persistent construction defects litigation and high insurance premiums remain major obstacles to office-to-residential conversions. The Downtown Denver Development Authority recently paid $37 million to acquire Denver Pavilions after it defaulted on its debt, a targeted public investment Mosher endorsed as critical to stabilizing the 16th Street corridor.

stories.headline: United Airlines expands Denver pilot training center, plans second campus near DIA
stories.summary:
United Airlines on Thursday celebrated the completion of the first phase of a major expansion at its Denver Flight Training Center at 7500 E. 35th Ave., adding 40 new CAE training devices since 2022. The facility now spans eight buildings and nearly 700,000 square feet and houses 86 CAE training devices, including 52 full-motion flight simulators. The center can train up to 860 pilots per day and conducts more than 32,000 training sessions annually.

All of United's nearly 18,000 pilots complete required simulator training at the Denver facility every nine months, making it the largest pilot training center in the world. CEO Scott Kirby and CAE CEO Matthew Bromberg spoke at the event, which was attended by U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper.

United also announced plans to break ground in 2027 on a second training facility on two parcels near Denver International Airport, with an expected opening around 2030. The airline purchased that land in 2023 for $33 million, and the Denver City Council approved rezoning the properties in July. The new facility will add additional flight simulators beyond the current center's capacity.

stories.headline: Cherry Creek's Truffle Cheese Shop to reopen in Denver's Golden Triangle under new ownership
stories.summary:
Truffle Cheese Shop, a 25-year-old Denver institution that lost its Cherry Creek storefront last October after the state seized its assets for back taxes, is set to reopen in the Golden Triangle neighborhood. Marketing entrepreneur David Walsh purchased a majority stake in the business in June and plans to reopen a 1,200-square-foot retail space at the Evans School later this year.

Former owner Lisa Morris, who bought the business in 2021 and has worked there since 2018, is staying on with a 20% ownership stake as the shop's creative director. Walsh and Morris say the tax issues that forced the original closure have been resolved.

The relaunched shop will carry the full range of products Truffle was known for, with plans to expand into kitchen goods and local producer features on a rotating basis. Walsh hopes to eventually add wine and beer on-site, pending city licensing, and is targeting a reopening before the holiday season — historically the shop's busiest period, accounting for roughly 35% of annual revenue.

stories.headline: Bo Nix sharp in preseason debut, scores on both drives in Broncos' loss to Green Bay
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix made a successful return from a fractured ankle Friday night, going 6-of-9 for 76 yards and a touchdown in the Broncos' 33-13 preseason loss to the Green Bay Packers at Empower Field. Nix, who had not played in a game since suffering the injury in January, connected with running back RJ Harvey on a 21-yard touchdown and hit new wide receiver Jaylen Waddle for a 35-yard gain during the starting unit's two-drive stint.

Head coach Sean Payton said after the game that Nix showed no restrictions and will be ready to go for the start of the regular season. New offensive coordinator and play-caller Davis Webb called plays for Nix for the first time in a game setting.

The Broncos' starters scored on both possessions, with the second drive ending in a 53-yard Wil Lutz field goal. Running back J.K. Dobbins, center Luke Wattenberg and wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr. dressed but did not play.

stories.headline: Nuggets sign six-time All-Star DeMar DeRozan to one-year, $3.9 million deal
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets are signing veteran guard DeMar DeRozan to a one-year minimum contract worth $3.9 million, according to multiple reports confirmed by ESPN's Shams Charania and The Athletic's Chris Haynes. The signing comes days after Denver traded Peyton Watson to the Cleveland Cavaliers in a sign-and-trade deal.

DeRozan, 37, is entering his 18th NBA season and ranks 16th all time in points scored with 26,711. He averaged 18.4 points, 4.1 assists and 2.9 rebounds per game for the Sacramento Kings last season while shooting 49.7% from the field. He is a six-time All-Star and three-time All-NBA selection.

With Denver's starting lineup unchanged from last season, DeRozan is expected to serve as a key reserve — a role he has rarely occupied in his career, having started 1,252 of his 1,264 career games. The signing brings the Nuggets to 14 of 15 standard roster spots filled.

stories.headline: Premier League Mornings Live Fan Festival coming to Denver's Union Station
stories.summary:
The Premier League has announced that its 13th Mornings Live Fan Festival will be held in Denver at Union Station, produced in collaboration with USA Sports and NBC Sports. The event is part of a traveling fan experience series that brings Premier League viewing parties and interactive activities to cities across the United States.

The Denver stop continues growing interest in soccer in the metro area, which has an established Major League Soccer presence with the Colorado Rapids. Specific dates and full programming details for the Union Station event were not immediately released.

The Premier League Fan Festival series has drawn large crowds at previous stops around the country, offering fans the opportunity to watch live matches on large screens alongside interactive displays and appearances tied to the league.

stories.headline: Denver-area heat, ozone alert Friday as temperatures approach 100 degrees
stories.summary:
The National Weather Service forecast temperatures near 98 degrees at Denver International Airport on Friday, approaching the all-time record high of 99 degrees set on Aug. 21, 2023. Areas along the I-25 corridor and Eastern Plains could see readings reach 100 degrees. The average high for this time of year in Denver is 87 degrees.

The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment issued an Ozone Action Day Alert through 4 p.m. for Denver and surrounding counties including Douglas, Jefferson, Arapahoe, Adams, Broomfield, Boulder, Larimer and Weld. Ozone levels were expected to reach unhealthy levels for people with respiratory conditions, and the broader Denver area was placed under a major heat risk advisory.

Meteorologists said there was a 20% chance of afternoon showers and thunderstorms after 3 p.m., with some isolated storms capable of producing wind gusts of 45 to 55 mph and hail on the Eastern Plains. Temperatures are expected to moderate to the low 90s over the weekend.

weather.notable: Nearly 9 degrees above the average high for this time of year.
